Well, we in this Party favour an intensification of the punishment of fines and imprisonment for those who profiteer in this way to get around or break Canadian law. If the goal is or ought to be
the putting to an end of that kind of profiteering and the effective curbing of some of the abuses, one would have hoped that the Bill we have before us would deal effectively with that. It does not deal with profiteering as such at all. It contains a provision which could lead to the imprisonment or imposition of serious fines on church people, representatives of Amnesty International, or other totally sincere and empathic human beings who are devoting a good part of their lives to try to facilitate the entry into Canada of legitimate refugees.
I do not say that lightly and I want to read into the record Clause 95.1 of the Bill which clearly makes this possible. It says this:
Every person who knowingly organizes, induces, aids or abets or attempts to organize, induce, aid or abet the coming into Canada of a person who is not in possession of a valid and subsisting visa, passport or travel document where one is required by this Act or the regulations is guilty of an offence and is liable-
It goes on to talk about prison sentences and fines up to the multi-thousand dollar level. I want to make a couple of points about that. First, most legitimate refugees who came to this country in recent years from Central America had no documents and could not get them. If they went to get them in a number of countries in Central America they would be put in jail or worse, so they arrive without them. They are arriving, perhaps even as we are debating now, with the aid of tremendously concerned church people.
According to my reading of this provision, the church people are subject to the penalties under the law. That is totally unacceptable to the members of my Party.
Hear, hear!

There is now an agreement for this measure to be in committee by Friday of this week. We will move a number of very specific amendments there. However, I will make a suggestion now which I hope the Government will begin considering. I assume the Government had good motives in terms of getting at the abuse associated with profiteering and wrong-doing of that kind, and that there was bad drafting of the legislation. I will put it that way. If that is the case, in my judgment there should be no reference at all to documentation being required for these refugees and we should get to the real problem. I suggest that instead of Clause 95(1) we ought to be considering in principle wording such as the following:
Every person who knowingly organizes, induces, aids or abets, or attempts to organize, induce, aid or abet a person to come into Canada in a clandestine manner, or to make a false refugee claim, is guilty of an offence.
If a person commits an offence fitting within this category, he or she should be liable to the punishments included in other sections of the Bill. That would mean that the church person, who is acting in good faith, or refugees who have no documents, would not be punished by the laws of Canada. We do not want to punish refugees. We want genuine refugees to be acceptable to this country.
August 12, 1987
Hear, hear!

I now want to turn to a third area of concern which Canadians have had. Canadians are concerned about the admission of people who might indeed be a security risk in our country or people who have committed major crimes in their land of origin. 1 would like to make a couple of points on this issue.
First, 1 understand international reality reasonably well on the point of serious security risk type of people. They are not the type of people who come as refugees. As the Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) said the other day, it is much more likely that such terrorists, such evil people, if 1 can put it that way, will come in with all the documents, wearing expensive suits and, quite conceivably, flying first class in an airplane. They will come in well organized, not as refugees.
Second, 1 did some checking and 1 believe I am right that there is no record in Canadian history of the Government ever finding a person who is deemed to be a security risk who came into Canada and applied as a refugee. My understanding is that no person who turned out to be a terrorist or serious criminal has ever actually applied within Canada as a refugee.
That having been said, all members of all Parties of course want to do everything they can to ensure that no such people come into our country. My Party is as concerned about that as is the Government.
At present a refugee claimant who is detained because of suspicion that he or she would fit into this category is entitled to a hearing within 48 hours. Subsequently the Security Intelligence Review Committee would be asked to determine whether there is a valid reason for this detention. That is the existing law. On the whole, this process, in terms of this category of person, seems to be a good one. However, Bill C-84 proposes replacing the Security Intelligence Review Committee with the judgment of the Federal Court.
There are two serious things wrong with that. One, it is the Security Intelligence Review Committee which has some expertise in passing judgment about security risks. That is why we created the agency. That is why we are in the process of building up a cadre of people with some expertise in this field. They have the expertise and presently have the responsibility of making a recommendation. However, the Government does not want to use the people with expertise but wants to give the responsibility to the Federal Court, which has no expertise whatsoever in this area. I am sure that any judge would candidly admit that. We are going to turn it over to a federal judge who has no expertise.
The second point is that, as everyone knows, there is a backlog at the Federal Court level of many months. The Federal Courts are also overburdened. Therefore, it again seems to us that the legitimate goal of dealing with potential terrorists and taking steps to stop their entry has not been achieved in a sensible way by replacing the Security Intelligence Review Committee's work with that of the Federal
Immigration Act, 1976
Court. That is a recommendation which we in this Party find lacks any sense whatsoever and one we cannot support.
I want to conclude my brief observations on this Bill by saying that we want abuses in the refugee system of our country stopped. We want profiteers punished. We certainly want terrorists to be stopped from entering Canada. However, we want these problems dealt with in ways consistent with the rule of law, with our own Charter of Rights, and with the Canadian tradition which has shown an openness to refugees. We cannot support the present Bill precisely because it violates these requirements.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner).

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a point of order before the Minister speaks. I mentioned that I sent a letter to the Minister last February and that I had not received a reply.
I have just been informed that I did receive a detailed reply. I want to correct that.

Mr. Speaker, 1 want to thank the Hon. Member for correcting what was obviously an oversight. I indeed appreciate some of his comments which were very helpful. Perhaps they have already listened to what they want to hear, but I would be happy to share a few remarks with them.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. If there are any further conversations, I wish Hon. Members would have them behind the curtain.

Mr. Speaker, we are in the midst of a difficult and volatile situation. Recent occurrences compel the Government to enact legislation that will eliminate the abuse of our immigration laws.
What we have heard clearly is that queue jumping will not be tolerated. It is unfair that a claimant who is not a legitimate refugee can move to the head of a line. That undermines the system and it incites further abuse.
I can understand the frustration of many who have waited long periods of time, hoping that they can sponsor members of their family or others who do not meet the narrow constraints of our immigration policy. I understand those frustrations and, in fact, in his statement this week the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) gave hope to those who have older non-dependent children that very soon they will be able to bring them in to join them. We know how important it is for them to be reunited with their families.
The current system of the refugee determination process is absurd. It is chaotic, it is unfair, and it just does not work. I hear some proposing a system that is even more complicated. We do not have an appeal process on merit now and some are

August 12, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
raising the possibility of a new system that establishes an appeal on merit. One wonders how that will function any better when we already have a system that does not function now.
Clearly we need a system that is firm, fair, just, and balances reason with compassion. It has to be able to identify and welcome real refugees. It must be able to provide protection to those who need protection.
There are others who have been making inappropriate refugee claims. There are illegal migrants-certainly good people-who are attempting to abuse our system.
Recently we have seen an increase in that abuse. Since May of last year only about 10 per cent of those claimants have been found to be legitimate refugees, according to the best advice of our refugee status advisory committee. In the previous year at least a third of the same claimants were deemed to be bona fide refugees. This indicates an increased abuse.
What does this mean to the real refugees of the world, and how are Canadians to perceive how their resources are being abused when they could be a benefit to real refugees?
This is a serious matter. W'e are sending out a strong message. It is that trafficking in human flesh cannot be accepted. It is deplorable, and that kind of smuggling, keeping people in sub-human conditions and forcing them to risk their lives, will be stopped. We will put those people who mass market in that way out of business.
It could be tragic if we allowed this to go on much longer. The tragedy would be that it could corrode the environment in which we must continue to operate a refugee policy. We need a more hospitable environment in order to build a more generous refugee policy and indeed bring an increasing number of immigrants to this country. As other Members have indicated, immigrants and refugees have made an enormous contribution to the wellbeing of this country. They create jobs, rather than remove them, and make an enormous contribution in terms of goods and services that they require.
Some Hon. Members have raised the security situation. I want to assure all Canadians that if there are reasonable grounds for believing that an individual is a danger to our society, or the person has committed a crime elsewhere, that person should not be permitted to make a refugee claim in this country. That position is supported by our international obligations and by our own Immigration Act.
We will continue to consider the reality. The fact that there are those who are not playing by the rules of the game has eroded public support. By welcoming and identifying real refugees, by removing unfounded claimants, by protecting legitimate refugees and deterring abusive claimants, we will send out a clear message to Canadians that in the summer of 1987 we heard their plea and that abuse will never be tolerated in this country.
1 want to explain the details of the new Bill and emphasize a few points before I do so. This legislation will bring in tough controls and some severe penalties. I will not deny that they are indeed tough, but this toughness is tempered by fairness and concern for refugees that has won Canada an international humanitarian reputation.
These proposals address a problem that has been brewing for the last few years. The arrival of the Sikhs is only the latest manifestation of this issue.
The number of refugee claims made at Canadian border crossings has increased dramatically in the last several years. In 1981, 3,450 claims were made. By 1986, that number ballooned to 18,000. An estimated 30,000 claims will be made by the end of this year.
Many of these claims are false and are clogging our refugee determination system. These measures will deter people who make false claims for refugee status from entering Canada.
This Government believes that tough deterrents will bring results.
What are we trying to do? The answer is simple. We want to prevent abuse of the refugee determination system. This will help genuine refugees to get fast, efficient assistance from Canada. We will help those who need our protection, not those who do not.
Bill C-55, which provides permanent solutions, was introduced in the House last May. Given the urgent human dimension of its recommendations, I would hope that the Opposition will consider Bill C-55 more objectively than it did last spring. It is landmark legislation that will streamline the claims process, provide expanded refugee hearing resources, make the determination process more efficient from top to bottom, and give Government new clout to dispatch economic migrants to safe third countries.

As for our motivation, we are deeply concerned by the unscrupulous smugglers who help people come illegally into Canada. Their activity is unacceptable. Not only is it unfair to those who pay their money on the strength of false promises, but it also jeopardizes human lives.
This is not only unfair to the people directly involved, but odious for all Canadians. We have to put an end to this practice and we shall do so. Experience has shown that existing penalties are not sufficiently harsh to deter smugglers.
The Bill introduced today provides appropriate penalties. Anyone who organizes or abets the smuggling of people into Canada is liable to a maximum prison term of five years and a maximum fine of $500,000.
The new provisions will make the activities of smugglers and merciless advisors more risky. Harsh penalties will also apply to the illegal disembarking of passengers in Canadian territorial waters. Our purpose is simple: We shall attack the
August 1 2, 1987

problem by making lawbreakers lose the benefits they could reap from their activities.
Transportation companies also carry responsibility for allowing people to enter Canada illegally. Some individuals enter Canada clandestinely, but the vast majority of improperly documented arrivals come on scheduled carriers.
Some transportation companies have been unwilling or apparently unable to ensure that their passengers carry proper travel documents. The Bill promises heavier fines for companies transporting people who do not have proper documentation. A fine of $5,000 for each passenger without proper travel documents will be imposed. The Deputy Minister of Employment and Immigration will have the power to require any company to deposit a security for unpaid fines. Failure to comply may result in the seizure of the company's planes. Under this legislation airlines will be permitted to collect documents and return them to individuals upon arrival in Canada.
In addition, transportation companies will collect information to help identify passengers who conceal or destroy their documents. The Government recognizes that limitations must be placed on the liability of airlines and other transportation companies. We recognize that the Government is obliged to deal with inadmissible persons quickly. Transportation companies do have responsibilities and obligations-which 1 am confident they will meet.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, many of the recent illegal arrivals came without identification. We need to improve our ability to detain improperly documented claimants until their identities can be established. This is important for two reasons. We have to be careful not to admit anyone who poses a threat to Canada's security; and we must be able to identify people who really do not need our protection.
Under the new legislation people arriving at major ports of entry without proper documentation will be detained for a period of up to seven days. If, after seven days, the senior immigration officer can demonstrate that reasonable efforts are being made to establish the claimant's identity, there is an obligatory extension for a further 21 days. Extensions beyond this 28-day period can be made weekly.
This measure sounds quite tough. It is. If we do not know who a person is then we do not know if that person is or is not dangerous. Simply put, we must know whom we are allowing into the country.
The need to establish identity is an important security precaution. A firmer detention policy is essential in any serious attempt to deter large influxes of bogus claimants. Once again I must emphasize that our aim here is to deter people from coming to Canada illegally.
Immigration Act, 1976
An important aspect of the legislation allows for the detention of security threats until they can be removed. In cases suggesting a criminal background based upon confidential information, a Minister's certificate describing this evidence will be presented to the immigration adjudicator. The inquiry will then be adjourned. The Minister's certificate will be presented to a justice of the Federal Court. The claimant will be given an opportunity to respond to the Minister's allegations. If the justice of the Federal Court rules that the claimant is a threat, then the person will be removed. That person will not have recourse to the refugee determination system.

Mr. Speaker, I have been outlining some of the punitive aspects of this Bill. I emphasize that these are deterrent provisions. The previous legislation left too much room for abuses. The entire world now knows that Canada will no longer tolerate such abuses.
The new legislation also provides other means of deterring fraudulent applicants. Naturally, many people want to take advantage of the economic opportunities offered by Canada, but we cannot allow them to cheat and to bypass regular immigration channels.
The government is now facing a difficult situation. The refugee determination process has bogged down. To date, five years are needed to establish whether a refugee claim is genuine. During that time, the claimant is entitled to work in Canada. If the tribunal rejects the claim, it is very difficult to send the individual back to his or her country of origin after all that time.

Over the last five years some 40,000 claimants came to our door and, as was their right, they made a refugee status claim. After the seven other levels of appeal and re-appeal, only some 650 were asked to leave the country. That is not a refugee determination process-it is a licence to abuse. It is a licence to come in by the back door. It is unfair. What all Canadians want is a system that is fair and just. If the criteria are well established, then let everyone have the same opportunity to meet them. Some people should not be able to jump into a third line which is totally unrelated to the immigration line, or to jump into a line that must always be there for true refugees, those people who need protection and who should always find a home here.

An individual may have a steady job, have started a family and have children who are Canadian citizens. This however does not legalize the way he or she entered Canada and is a breach by economic migrants of established immigration rules.
Mr. Speaker, the current process, if I may say so, is an invitation to abuse. It is therefore clear that we need a more effective and expeditious system. This legislation is a major

August 12, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
and necessary step in that direction. Expeditious treatment will deter illegitimate refugee claims.

There is no better deterrent than a much more expeditious determination process. Once those people who are known not to be refugees whose claims are either manifestly unfounded, who have refugee status and who have lived sufficient lengths of time elsewhere, who can be returned to those countries or who can seek the protection of those countries are removed from the system, then that will send the clearest message to people around the world that it does not pay to sell all of one's belongings and pick up and try to hit Canada as an illegal alien. Indeed, it may be more appropriate and beneficial to those people to try to apply under the regulation, under the immigration stream. Indeed, most of these people have not done that.

People are more reluctant to take fraudulent actions if they know they can be removed rapidly, and we already have evidence of that.

Canada is an open and caring country. All of us are very fortunate to live here. We are privileged to claim Canada as our home. This is no secret to the rest of the world. Our international reputation as a land of peace and opportunity is what impresses people and makes them want to live here. And we want them to come. We will be increasing immigration levels over the next three years. I take pride in the international reputation Canada enjoys as a safe haven for refugees. It is an honour that hard work and dedication have won.
We steadfastly maintain our commitment not only to immigrants but to refugees. At least 17,000 refugees will enter Canada by the end of this year. Obviously, the attraction of Canada has led some people to attempt to bypass regular immigration channels. This worsening situation has prompted the Government to introduce deterrent measures to prevent abuse now.
We want to ensure that there is time for a full and reasoned debate of Bill C-55 to chart the path for refugee determination for some years to come. This Bill is designed to address immediate and difficult circumstances to stop the most flagrant abuses. Bill C-55 seeks to address long-term issues which are facing us. The Government is faced with a difficult situation. Responsible action is needed now and will be needed again in order to pass Bill C-55.
The task before us is one which transcends partisanship. It concerns fundamental issues of fairness, justice, and the integrity of our laws. As such it is a task which deserves not only the attention of all Hon. Members, it demands action. It demands our collective resolve and determination to deal expeditiously with these deterrent and detention measures.
I urge all Hon. Members to accept this challenge, and in so doing to take a major step toward ensuring that Canada will have a refugee determination system that is truly effective, responsive and just.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: On questions and comments, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell).

The Hon. Member from Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) made a strong case for the possibility that caring Canadians who are trying to help legitimate refugees could be charged and prosecuted under this Act. Is the Government prepared to look at that clause and to accept the appropriate amendment?

I indicated that I appreciated many of the thoughtful remarks of the Leader of the New Democratic Party, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent). I have not had a chance to study in great detail what he has asked, or what he is offering. Certainly, I accept and welcome the contribution from him and other Members of Parliament. That is what this process is all about. Nothing has been cast in stone. We are certainly most willing and interested. There is an urgency to the situation. We must send out a message that we will be passing this Bill as quickly as possible. This Bill is to deter, detain, and deport in certain instances, and I would be very pleased to be able to observe and bring it forward in the manner that is prescribed.

It may help the Minister if I brought to his attention the point that has been raised, namely, that the Minister proposes in Section 95.1 to imprison a Canadian, a group, an organization, or a group within a church that engages in helping prospective refugees who may be without documents, and who may want to come into Canada. I am referring specifically to Section 95.1.
Would the Minister be more explicit and indicate to us whether he will accept an amendment that will take into account the number of organizations, churches, and individuals who seek, in the cause of helping potential refugees, a very legitimate activity under the Canadian system?

For almost 10 years there has been a section in the Immigration Act, and I wish to quote Section 95(m). It states that the present Act includes the following offence:
Every person who (m) knowingly induces, aids or abets or attempts to
induce, aid or abet any person to contravene any provision of this Act or the
regulations, is guilty of an offence and is liable
The provision was always there, but obviously this was not intended to affect church people and non-governmental organization workers, and we share with them their dedicated interest to help real refugees. What we are attempting to do by the specifics of this provision is to get at the organizers of clandestine movements, those that deal with the mass marketing of human misery. Those are the people we want to put out of business.
August 12, 1987

The specifics are such that we have taken three definitions from the original Act. We have combined them here. What there is in the specific definitions, 95.1 and 95.2 was already covered by the generalities of 95(m). In the past 10 years we have not prosecuted a single person who was a member of a church or non-governmental organization for his or her legitimate activity. But if it is illegitimate activity, and if they are contravening the Act and mass marketing this type of misery, obviously they too should pay the price.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: This afternoon we heard speeches from the Opposition which stated that the new laws proposed in both Bill C-55 and Bill C-84 were destroying the credibility of our immigration system. I wish to ask the Minister if he feels that this is true. Does he agree that the abuses which were increasing in alarming numbers over the last number of years were causing the credibility gap with our very generous and fair immigration system, and a very serious backlash was starting to develop here that could destroy what we have built up over the last number of years?

In 1987 we will be welcoming 125,000 immigrants and refugees to Canada. These are people who will meet the criteria either under our independent immigrant class, business investors and entrepreneurs which are a small part of the program, family reunification, and 20,000 refugees and humanitarian cases.
When people who do not meet the criteria come anyway as they have been doing in increasing numbers, there have been over 16,000 this year, we know that over 90 per cent of them are non-legitimate refugees. They are people who should be applying in other streams. They should be applying as immigrants. This causes a frustration in communities with people who have been waiting to sponsor their relatives. 1 said that I understood that frustration and I understood why they are having difficulty waiting. The trouble it is causing in the community is that it is leading to a feeling that maybe accepting immigrants and refugees is not what we should be doing. I look out and say that there has to be a positive benefit to this. The positive benefit is to put your house in order, stop that abuse, stop illegal aliens. We say no to illegal aliens, and yes to real refugees.
At the same time let us give ourselves the opportunity to focus on the enormous contribution that immigrants and refugees make to this society. In 1986 alone, the 100,000 people who came here contributed over $2.25 billion to the economic development of this country. That is a gigantic contribution. All of them continue to make that contribution. They are not the ones who are out of work. They are the ones who are creating jobs, and by their purchases of goods and services they are helping to advance this society to allow us to continue to grow. I say that by being firm and fair and by creating this type of an environment, we can be assured that this hospitable environment-after 1 have cleared up the policy matter, created a better understanding of what refugees and immigrants are, and stopped illegal aliens-will allow a much
Immigration Act, 1976
broader growth of the immigration program, and will allow us to be more generous to real refugees. We are making a tremendous commitment to refugees. On a per capita basis, Canada does more for the real refugees of the world than any other country.

My question is directed to the Minister. Yesterday I received a telegram from within my riding from the Redemptionist Fathers. They were expressing understandable concern about the rather Draconian tone of the present Bill C-84. It seems to many that the Bill has already caused a lot of concern among groups. I know that the Minister would not wish to encourage concern if there is a way to deal with the matter. In trying to make Canadians feel that the Government at last is coming to grips with a subject on which it has perhaps delayed too long, perhaps it is now trying to come up with something that is so Draconian and so severe that it will satisfy everyone's concerns. That is not a very healthy way to proceed. I wonder whether the Minister is prepared to do something about Sections 95.1 and 95.2.
In terms of not only religious communities but all those concerned about fairness, as I think are all Canadians, what is the Minister doing to assure Canadians that steps will not be taken or laws will not be passed that can implicate people who are working for refugees in a positive way in a Bill which is supposed to be trying to deal with only those who are genuinely exploiting the refugee situation?

Mr. Speaker, I hope everybody is clearly getting the message that we abhor the trafficking in human flesh. That process must stop. Very clearly our message of deterrence is being well received.
Perhaps the transportation companies will get the same message-$5,000 for every undocumented arrival. We want them to collect documents and we will authorize them to do it. We want to ensure that the people they bring here will be available to us in a way that we can get an understanding of where they come from and who they are.
We are not meaning to affect any individual who has dedicated his life and work to the real refugees of the world. However, we are going to stop this organized movement of clandestine groups who want to abuse us and take us for patsies. Canadians have said "no more", and we are speaking out loudly and clearly. Saying "no" to illegal aliens will still give us the right to say "yes" to real refugees and to do well.

Mr. Speaker, thank you very much for recognizing me and for giving me the opportunity to follow the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) who, from the comments he has been making in the last 30 minutes, is obviously suffering from an acute case of schizophrenia.

August 12, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
On the one hand he says that Canadians are proud of the traditions and accomplishments in making this an open, tolerant, and generous country. Then he bangs his fist on the desk and says, "By God, we are going to stop all this kind of nonsense from coming forth", and begins waving the xenophobic flags and saying that we will not tolerate any more flagrant violations of the system.
Right on!
Exactly.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, why don't you call them to order over there?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: It has been a great debate this afternoon on this particular Bill. We still have about seven minutes remaining. I hope courtesy would be extended to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy).

I think we should pose some questions to that Minister and his boss, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard). If they truly believe that Canada has established leadership in this issue, why is it that they have introduced legislation which clearly contravenes all the international obligations we have signed since 1969? Why have they introduced legislation which caused the United Nations High Commission on Refugees to take the unprecedented step of sending an aide-memoire to the Government saying, "What you are doing is wrong"?
Did you see it and what it says?

Yes. That is exactly what it says. I have it right here.
Why is it that the United Nations High Commission said on the matter of transportation that to put the responsibility of determining who is a refugee on a private commercial airline which is untrained, as opposed to recognizing the responsibility of a country to determine the fundamental issue of who should be a member of its community, is against the convention on refugees? That is, again, from international authorities.
We could cite statement after statement, evidence after evidence, to show that the Government is flagrantly transgressing the commitment of our country to the international community. It is deliberately going against the steps we have taken as a country to support an international refugee system which tries to deal with one of the world's most serious and desperate problems.
There is no question that this is a problem which should occupy and demand the intelligence and response of all Canadians. We are a country which knows what it might be like to be homeless. Many of us come from families who were kicked out of their own countries. Many of our families fled from persecution, famine, and Governments which treated them in a tyrannical manner.
Put yourself in the following position, Mr. Speaker. We in the House can speak confidently, but think of yourself, your wife, and your family if you did not belong anywhere, if you had no rights anywhere, if you were kicked around from country to country.
I have met those kinds of people in the refugee camps of the world. I have talked with them. 1 know the desperation one can see in their eyes. It is no wonder they try to get here.
We have heard people talk about queue-jumpers and illegal aliens as if they were somehow criminally sponsored. They are people looking for a home, a place to belong, where they have some roots and some rights.
This country, to its credit and up to the last year, has led the world in trying to ensure that there was a fair system to deal with that problem. We undertook international negotiations beginning in 1983 with the Americans, the Europeans, and the Asians to try to find a way in which to share the burden. At that time we saw the beginning of Berlin walls for refugees around the world, the beginning of restrictive measures. We said to the international community: "This must stop. We must find a way of sharing the responsibility and a way of organizing ourselves as an international community to deal with this kind of problem". By the way, the present Government no longer follows that initiative. In fact it was dropped as part of its foreign policy agenda.
When they say, "Why didn't we find a solution", I say, "Why didn't the Minister and his predecessor follow that initiative to try to get international co-operation and fight against restrictive measures rather than go the opposite way and become a follower, following the worst examples rather than setting the best example."
Hear, hear!

He says, "We appeal to find some solution to the problem in Canada". These solutions have been sitting on desks of the the Minister and his predecessor for over two years. The Plaut Commission, commissioned by the previous Government, was put forward as a way of clearly responding to a reform of the refugee determination system. It was then examined by a Commons committee with a majority of Conservative Members who came up with a unanimous report, which the Government ignored, as it ignored the Plaut Commission.
As if that were not enough, the former Chairman, the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), called a meeting last December of NGOs, Amnesty International, UNHCR, and officials of the Department, and came up with a consensus decision.
Do we not hear from the Government all the time, "Let's find a consensus agreement, let's find a way of doing things that is commonly shared"? They had an arrangement to which the churches, refugee organizations, the UN, and Amnesty International agreed. Only one group did not agree; the
August 12, 1987

Minister and his officials did not agree. They were the only ones who stood against that consensus. They were the only ones who stood against the kind of solution which enjoys the total approbation of all interested parties in this country.
What was the problem? Why is it that only they are in step? Why is it that only they have the divine ordinance to tell who is a real refugee?
It is heresy for a Minister of Immigration to stand in the House and say, "I know who is a legitimate refugee, and we are going to keep the bad ones out". We have established in this country an independent process, a process immune from that kind of political influence, to ensure that refugees would have a fair, impartial, and independent hearing. Now we have Ministers of Immigration who are saying that they want to take it back unto their fold. They want to decide who are refugees. They want to decide whether it is the colour of their skin or their hair or their religion which determines whether they are bona fide refugees. They are corrupting that system, and they are going to hear more from me tomorrow morning on that. That is what they are engaged in-corruption of the system, and they know it.
One of the real responsibilities of the Minister of Immigration, rather than inflaming public opinion and rather than
Immigration Act, 1976
generating the kind of response we have seen, is to try to educate and to make Canadians understand the problems they face. It is a sensitive, delicate responsibility. It is a responsibility which has been kicked in the teeth by the present Minister of Employment and Immigration and his assistant. They do not recognize the responsibility to ensure that there is a balance between the system of proper recognition of civil liberties of Canadians and of refugees and making sure that the system works efficiently.
You will hear more about that tomorrow morning, Mr. Speaker.
Hear, hear!
